lines.english: Looking up, I see the same hollow sky. The same old sky I've been averting my eyes from for the past five years.
The same old sky that now watches over the aftermath of those dreamlike, happy days filled with so much pain.
"Hey."
"Hey."
Beyond the door of the hospital room, I'm met with a rather curt answer.
Of course, that's only because my greeting was curt as well.
"Here, souvenirs."
"Where did you buy these?"
A dull room decorated with nothing but empty flower pots. Though, since neither the patient nor the visitor have any interest in flowers, I don't see the problem.
"You like these, right? Frozen mandarins."
Because any time spent taking care of flowers is time not spent devouring fruits. Of course, it's not the fruit itself that is valuable, but the sugar contents.
"Wait a second, this thing is frozen solid. I can't peel the skin off this thing."
"Then let me do it for you."
"Don't be ridiculous. A pianist shouldn't be getting her fingers all yellow."
"I really don't see the problem…"
In the only place for miles where Japanese is mutually understood, we can finally relax a little.
This is my hour of comfort, coming only once a day.
However…
"What is it? Why are you staring at me?"
"No, it's nothing."
It's only by a little bit, but it looks like she's lost weight again.
"Anyway, how are you feeling?"
Mom mutters those words as if she just remembered them, the frozen mandarin still in her mouth.
"You're the patient. Those words should be directed at you, not at me…"
"Where's the fun in hearing about how sick a sick person is? It's your piano that's important."
"Well, it's going decent… I guess?"
I toss a piece into my own mouth as well, and bite the crunchy chilliness which before long completely permeates my teeth.
…This freezer is way too good at freezing.
"But your massive success in Japan made you the star of the hour. You shouldn't be wasting the opportunity."
"But the first concert was a total failure. It was only during the additional concert that I managed to salvage the disaster somewhat."
"All's well that ends well. In fact, it was partially due to the mediocre first performance that the massive improvement in the second made so much noise."
"Being a pianist, I can't say that evaluation makes me happy. It's like you're telling me 'You don't know unless you try!' or something."
"Well it's true, you really don't know unless you try. If you don't like it then try being more consistent. Practice 50 or 100 hours a day if you have to."
"If you can provide me with such incredible power, then by all means, boss."
"Have you ever heard of the hyperbolic time chamber? For now I've figured out the theoretical part to make one, but I haven't started the experiments yet."
When I have these carefree conversations with my mom, it's almost as if we're back in Japan…
No, it goes even further back than our homecoming. It's as if she hasn't changed one bit.
However…
"I'm sorry."
"Indeed, a frozen mandarin must have a thin coating of ice on the surface, but the peel and contents themselves must be slightly soft…"
"I'm sorry for making you come back to Vienna… because of my selfishness."
"…I was really hoping you'd join me in my critique of these mandarins."
A week after my flight from Japan…
After finishing up the last of her business, Mom also left.
…Of course, she didn't really get to finish her business there.
She simply chased after me so she could protect me. She finally abandoned Japan for my sakeーwithout even considering her own condition.
She did it all for me, even at the cost of abandoning her modest wish of spending her last days in Japan.
"I'll do anything. I won't be fussy, I'll come to visit you every day, and I'll even do as you say… so please…"
"How many times do I have to tell you this? If you want to please me, then play your piano. Don't say 'it's going decent' at a time like this."
"Mom…"
"Besides, I don't regret coming back here. The place I belong is wherever my beloved daughter lives. I can finally come to terms with that now…"
When I first found out about the truth, here in Vienna, my emotions were a mix of despair, unease and grief.
I understood why Mom was so obsessed with the idea of a concert in Japan. I understood why she wanted me to shine in that country.
When I managed to connect the dots, I began to hate myself.
I lost the little love I had for the idiotic daughter who trampled all over her mother's determination, all because of some childish heartbreak.
The notion that the selfishness that brought my mom back to Vienna might have… hastened the approach of 'that time'…
"R-Right! I had an exam here just earlier, at this hospital."
"So, did it turn out positive? Will I become a grandmother?"
"You were practically making me cry just moments ago. Why can't you stay serious for more than a few seconds?"
"What do you mean? This is something that would have a massive impact on your life."
"In any case, that's not what I'm talking about. Listen to me carefully."
…It didn't turn out positive.
So please, don't bring that up again.
Just let me move on…
"It was a compatibility test. For a marrow transplant."
Instead, I will put all my effort into the things I am capable of.
The one form of filial piety I am capable of.
"They said the results will come in later. Wait until then, would you?"
"If we're compatible… no, I'm sure it'll be fine. When that happens, Mom, I'll…"
"…I won't allow it."
"Huh…?"
Whenever I put in the effort, it usually leads me in the wrong direction. I know that much from experience…
"You've clearly spent a lot of time researching my illness, but I never knew you were considering something so idiotic."
"What do you mean, idiotic!?"
"It means precisely what you think it means. Don't do idiotic things, you idiot!"
Even so, Mom's words were no small shock to me, as for this one instance, I genuinely believed that I was making the right decision.
"You're the idiot here!
"And so what?"
"It means that it'd be more absurd not to do the test. If we're compatible, then you'll be able to…"
"Even if we're compatible, I'll never allow it."
"Why!?"
"No matter what."
"That's no reason at all!"
"Stop making a scene in the hospital. They'll throw you out."
"How can I not make a scene!? You have such a great possibility right in front of you, so why would you just…"
"I would never agree to anything that would hurt you…"
That's right…
It's only when I have those carefree conversations with my mom, that it feels as if nothing has changed.
"I will never allow any decision that would cause any harm to the body, talent, or the nerves of the pianist Touma Kazusa."
"What are you saying…? I'd obviously be perfectly fine…"
"I won't allow the slightest risk. It can never be allowed to happen…"
"M-Mom…"
But as much as it feels like nothing has changed…
"No one has the right to take my one single hope away from me."
"But I'm…!"
"Even if that's what you yourself want, I won't allow it."
"I won't allow it, Kazusa…"
As of this moment, my mom just loves me far too much.
She's envisioning me as her own successor.
She's already picturing a world where she no longer exists…
"Ah…"
As I exit the hospital, I'm greeted by the same hollow sky.
A sky even more lost than during noon, as if reflecting the feelings of my heart. A sky at the end of a long dream.
But reality goes on even after one wakes from a dream.
A reality cruel beyond anything that preceded it. All because I've had a lifetime's worth of happiness…
